newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Labour makes pitch to traditional supporters.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Labour makes pitch to traditional supporters.

text.p: Labour Leader Helen Clark kicked off her party's election campaign in Auckland on Sunday with a strong pitch aimed at Labour's traditional support base.

Clark, whose party has struggled to overcome the memories of the reformist Labour Government of 1984-90, made a pitch to the underprivileged, the underpaid, unions, Maori and Pacific Islanders. She promised a return to a more supportive government in the key areas of education, health and welfare.
The slick opening to around 600-700 supporters bore all the hallmarks of a cultural festival, complete with Maori and Pacific Island entertainment.
The Labour leader began by lamenting the plight of the poor under the current National Government.
Auckland's City Mission, she said, was now serving 20,000 free meals a year compared with just 8,000 in the depths of the depression.
"But distress in this country doesn't begin and end with the very poor. It is right through our community."
Clark asked what had happened to quality health care.
"That has all been destroyed by people who know the costs of everything and the value of nothing," she said.
Teachers, social workers, nurses and the police were under terrific strain as they bore the brunt of an "increasingly aggressive and abusive underclass".
Labour, she said, was all about well thought out, measured and substantial policies of change.
Clark accused the governing National Party of listening only to big business.
The Employment Contracts Act, which allows wage bargaining between employee and employer, would be scrapped as Labour stood for stood for the right of workers to have a voice through their unions.
Maori would also get support for health services in their communities as would Pacific Island groups.
Accident Compensation would be restored to its former self, with a return of lump sum payments.

"We want a confident, secure New Zealand which can take on the world. We can be the Swiss of the South Pacific. But what's holding New Zealand back is pennypinching and blind ideology in education and training."
Unlike New Zealand First, Labour was strongly committed to foreign investment as an important part of job creation.
Clark said MMP was bringing a great change in the political system -- and no political party was unaffected by it.
"You can take National backed up by the Christian Coalition and the extremists in Act or you can take Labour, which will reach out to other opposition parties to form a government.

"Only Labour, of all the alternatives in this new, competitive political market place, has the substance and the people to lead the change which will turn this country around. And cry your heart out Jim Bolger, we will not enter a coalition with National." -- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
